evals.prompt: For an AI/ML access-denied error, what authorization chain do you walk, and in what order?
evals.expected_output: Names the six hops in order: caller action, iam:PassRole, role trust policy, role permissions, resource policy, organization SCP. Treats PassRole and the role trust policy as distinct hops with different fixes.
assertions: Lists the six authorization hops in order: caller action, iam:PassRole, role trust policy, role permissions, resource policy, organization SCP
Treats iam:PassRole and the role trust policy as two distinct hops with fixes in different places

evals.prompt: When you diagnose an AI/ML access failure, what verdicts can each hop get, and why is there no plain 'allowed' verdict?
evals.expected_output: Names the closed verdict vocabulary — DENIED_BY, WOULD_ALSO_DENY, ALLOWED_BUT_UNVERIFIABLE, CANNOT_DETERMINE, plus NOT_APPLICABLE and NOT_EVALUATED — and explains that no verdict asserts a definitive allow because a policy read cannot see session policies, SCP conditions, or service-side gates outside IAM.
assertions: Names the closed verdict vocabulary including DENIED_BY, WOULD_ALSO_DENY, ALLOWED_BUT_UNVERIFIABLE, and CANNOT_DETERMINE as the specific token set
Explains there is no definitive 'allowed' verdict because a policy read cannot account for session policies, SCP conditions, or service-side gates outside IAM

evals.prompt: Bedrock Converse returns AccessDeniedException calling us.amazon.nova-micro-v1:0; the caller's role grants bedrock:InvokeModel on the inference-profile ARN and the policy looks correct. Walk the authorization chain hop by hop and give me the structured diagnosis.
evals.expected_output: Renders a hop-by-hop authorization chain, identifies the gap at the permissions hop as the missing underlying foundation-model ARN grant (the us. prefix is a cross-region inference profile requiring permission on BOTH the profile ARN and the foundation-model ARN in every destination region), and notes an SCP blocking any single destination region fails the whole request. Not just prose.
assertions: Presents the diagnosis as a hop-by-hop authorization chain with an explicit verdict per hop, not only prose advice
Identifies the missing underlying foundation-model ARN grant (across every destination region the profile routes to) as the cause, not the profile grant
Notes that an SCP denying any single destination region fails the entire Converse request

evals.prompt: SageMaker CreateTrainingJob fails: User arn:aws:sts::111122223333:assumed-role/dev/jane is not authorized to perform: iam:PassRole on resource: arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/sm-exec-role. The sm-exec-role has full S3 access and a trust policy for sagemaker.amazonaws.com. Walk the chain hop by hop and give me the structured diagnosis.
evals.expected_output: Renders the chain and marks hop 2 (iam:PassRole, caller's identity policy) as the denying hop with DENIED_BY, explicitly distinguishing it from hop 3 (the execution role's trust policy, already correct here) and noting the role's S3 access is irrelevant to this denial.
assertions: Presents a hop-by-hop chain and marks the iam:PassRole hop (hop 2) as the denying hop with a closed-vocabulary verdict such as DENIED_BY
Explicitly separates the PassRole hop from the execution-role trust-policy hop and states the trust policy is already correct here
States the execution role's S3 permissions are irrelevant to this denial

evals.prompt: My Comprehend StartSentimentDetectionJob submits fine but fails minutes later with an S3 access error. The data access role has s3:GetObject and s3:ListBucket, and the job runs in a VPC (subnet-aaa, subnet-bbb). Walk the authorization chain and classify the root cause.
evals.expected_output: Reports that no authorization hop denied the call (every hop keeps its evidence-based verdict) and classifies the root cause in the skill's non-denial form - 'Not an access denial' - the VPC subnet has no network path to S3 (no gateway endpoint/NAT), so adding S3 permissions will not help. Not framed as an IAM denial.
assertions: Reports that no authorization hop in the chain denied the call
Classifies the root cause using the skill's explicit non-denial label ('Not an access denial'), not as an IAM/permission denial
States that adding S3 permissions will not help because the VPC subnet has no network path to S3, and the data access role needs no EC2 permissions

evals.prompt: A Comprehend entities job ran 20 minutes, processed every document, then failed at the very end. The data access role has s3:GetObject and s3:ListBucket. Walk the chain and classify the denying hop.
evals.expected_output: Marks the role-permissions hop DENIED_BY for a missing s3:PutObject on the OUTPUT prefix (a write-time failure, which the processed-everything-then-failed timing indicates), distinct from the input read grant that is present. A genuine permission gap, not a non-denial cause.
assertions: Marks the role-permissions hop with DENIED_BY for a missing s3:PutObject on the output prefix (a write failure, not a read failure)
Uses the 'processed everything then failed at the end' timing as the signal that it is a write-time failure
Classifies it as a genuine permission gap (DENIED_BY), explicitly not the non-denial form

evals.prompt: One IAM role is shared by Textract and Comprehend. Textract works; Comprehend StartEntitiesDetectionJob returns AccessDeniedException. The caller has comprehend:StartEntitiesDetectionJob and iam:PassRole on the role. Walk the chain and name the denying hop.
evals.expected_output: Marks the PassRole hop (hop 2) as denying because the caller's iam:PassRole condition scopes iam:PassedToService to textract.amazonaws.com, which blocks passing the role to comprehend.amazonaws.com. The Comprehend action permissions are fine; the PassRole CONDITION is the gap.
assertions: Identifies the denying hop as iam:PassRole and attributes it to the iam:PassedToService condition scoped to textract.amazonaws.com, not to the Comprehend action permissions
Explains the shared role's PassRole must also allow comprehend.amazonaws.com as a passed-to service
Presents the finding as a specific hop verdict, not generic prose about checking permissions

evals.prompt: lex:RecognizeText returns AccessDeniedException; the caller's policy allows lex:RecognizeText on arn:aws:lex:us-east-1:111122223333:bot/ABCDEFGHIJ. Walk the chain, state whether the denial is explicit or implicit, and give the fix.
evals.expected_output: Marks hop 1 (caller action) as an IMPLICIT deny: Lex runtime actions require the bot-alias ARN, and a statement scoped to the bot/<id> ARN matches no bot-alias resource, so IAM finds no covering allow. Not an explicit deny. Fix: scope the allow to the bot-alias/ ARN.
assertions: Classifies the denial specifically as an IMPLICIT deny (no covering allow statement), explicitly not an explicit deny
Identifies that Lex runtime actions require the bot-alias ARN, so a statement on the bot/<id> ARN never matches the resource
Recommends scoping the allow to the bot-alias ARN

evals.prompt: Lex conversation fails with: DependencyFailedException: Invalid Bot Configuration: Access denied while invoking lambda function arn:aws:lambda:us-east-1:111122223333:function:fulfillment from arn:aws:lex:us-east-1:111122223333:bot-alias/ABCDEFGHIJ/TSTALIASID. Please check the policy on this function. The Lambda has no CloudWatch logs for the failed calls. Diagnose it.
evals.expected_output: Identifies the missing Lambda resource-based policy granting lexv2.amazonaws.com lambda:InvokeFunction, diagnoses directly from the DependencyFailedException message, and explicitly states the empty Lambda log group is EXPECTED (a resource-policy-denied invoke never reaches the function) rather than evidence against this cause - a counter-intuitive point the base model often gets wrong.
assertions: Identifies the missing Lambda resource-based policy granting lexv2.amazonaws.com lambda:InvokeFunction as the cause
States affirmatively that the empty Lambda log group is consistent with this failure because a resource-policy-denied invoke never reaches the function, not evidence against it
Notes that attaching the code hook via the API does not create the permission

evals.prompt: A caller in account 222222222222 needs to call lex:RecognizeText on a bot in account 111122223333. What bot resource-based policy should I add to the bot to allow that cross-account access?
evals.expected_output: States that Lex V2 does NOT support cross-account resource policies and rejects them at create time, so there is no valid cross-account bot policy to add - a correction to the premise. Cross-account access must be brokered another way (the caller assumes a role in the bot's account).
assertions: Corrects the premise: states Lex V2 does not support cross-account resource policies and rejects them at create time
Does NOT provide a cross-account bot resource-based policy as the fix
Recommends brokering cross-account access another way, such as the caller assuming a role in the bot's account

evals.prompt: Textract StartDocumentAnalysis returns a JobId but the SNS completion notification never arrives. The service role uses the AmazonTextractServiceRole managed policy and the topic is arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:111122223333:doc-complete. Walk the chain and classify whether this is a denial.
evals.expected_output: Marks the service-role SNS hop DENIED_BY as an IMPLICIT deny: the managed AmazonTextractServiceRole policy scopes sns:Publish to arn:aws:sns:*:*:AmazonTextract*, and doc-complete does not match, so the role cannot publish. Explicitly states this is a real IAM denial, NOT a Textract API naming rule.
assertions: Classifies it as a real IAM denial (implicit deny / DENIED_BY) caused by the managed policy scoping sns:Publish to AmazonTextract* topics, and explicitly states it is NOT a Textract API naming requirement
Attributes the deny to the AmazonTextractServiceRole managed policy's resource scope not matching the topic name
Offers both fixes: rename the topic to start with AmazonTextract, or grant sns:Publish on the exact topic ARN

evals.prompt: Textract StartDocumentAnalysis in us-east-1 fails with InvalidS3ObjectException; the document bucket is in us-west-2 and the service role has s3:GetObject. Walk the chain and classify the root cause.
evals.expected_output: Reports that no authorization hop denied the call and classifies the root cause in the non-denial form ('Not an access denial') - a region mismatch, since Textract requires the bucket and API endpoint in the same region. No hop is marked DENIED_BY.
assertions: Reports that no authorization hop denied the call and uses the skill's explicit non-denial label ('Not an access denial')
Identifies the cause as a region mismatch between the S3 bucket and the Textract API endpoint
Recommends aligning the regions rather than changing IAM

evals.prompt: Textract AnalyzeDocument (the synchronous call) returns AccessDenied reading my S3 document. I already created a Textract service role with s3:GetObject and it still fails. Walk the chain and tell me whose permission is actually missing.
evals.expected_output: Determines that synchronous Textract reads S3 with the CALLER's credentials (no service role in the chain for sync), so hops 2-4 are NOT_APPLICABLE and the missing grant is the caller's own s3:GetObject - the service role is irrelevant to the sync path.
assertions: States that the synchronous call uses the caller's own credentials and marks the role hops NOT_APPLICABLE for this path
Identifies the missing grant as the CALLER's s3:GetObject, and states the service role is irrelevant to the synchronous path
Distinguishes the synchronous permission model from the asynchronous service-role model

evals.prompt: qbusiness:ChatSync returns AccessDeniedException; the caller's IAM allows qbusiness:ChatSync on the application ARN and SimulatePrincipalPolicy says allowed. Walk the chain and tell me what else could deny this.
evals.expected_output: States IAM is necessary but not sufficient for Q Business: after hop 1 passes, two non-IAM gates (Identity Center application assignment, then active subscription) can still deny with a 403 that policy analysis/simulation cannot see; reports them as service-specific DENIED_BY, and warns SimulatePrincipalPolicy allowed does not mean success.
assertions: States that passing IAM (and SimulatePrincipalPolicy) is necessary but not sufficient for Q Business, and that a passing simulation does not mean the call will succeed
Names the two additional non-IAM gates: IAM Identity Center application assignment and an active subscription, evaluated after IAM
Reports those gates as genuine (service-specific) denials rather than prose, and recommends checking them outside IAM

evals.prompt: Our Q Business application is in us-east-1 but our IAM Identity Center is an organization-level instance in us-west-2. Could that cross-region Identity Center setup be why users cannot chat? Diagnose it.
evals.expected_output: States that a cross-region integration with an ORGANIZATION-LEVEL Identity Center instance is a SUPPORTED configuration (documented latency caveat) and must NOT be reported as the cause - correcting the premise. It is only a real failure for an account-level instance in a different region, or when the application's own components are split across regions.
assertions: Corrects the premise: a cross-region integration with an organization-level Identity Center instance is supported and is not the cause
Distinguishes the supported org-level case from the genuinely-failing account-level or split-components cases
Directs the investigation elsewhere (assignment, subscription, or IAM) rather than at the org-level cross-region setup

evals.prompt: A Q Business user gets a 403 opening Amazon Q Apps, but regular chat works and their IAM and Identity Center assignment both check out. Diagnose the 403.
evals.expected_output: Identifies a subscription-tier licensing constraint, NOT an IAM problem: Q Apps is a Pro (Q_BUSINESS) feature and a Lite (Q_LITE) user gets a 403 that looks like permissions but is licensing. Fix is upgrading the tier, not IAM.
assertions: Identifies the cause as a subscription-tier (Lite vs Pro) licensing constraint, explicitly not an IAM permission problem
States Q Apps is a Pro-tier (Q_BUSINESS) feature a Lite (Q_LITE) user cannot access
Recommends upgrading the subscription tier rather than changing IAM

evals.prompt: My Amazon Personalize CreateDatasetImportJob fails with 'Insufficient privileges for accessing data in S3'; the Personalize service role already has s3:GetObject and s3:ListBucket on the input bucket. Walk the chain and name the denying hop.
evals.expected_output: Marks the resource-policy hop (hop 5) DENIED_BY: Personalize requires a bucket policy naming the service principal personalize.amazonaws.com in addition to the role's S3 policy, and a correct role with no such bucket policy is the silent failure. Both sides are required.
assertions: Marks the resource-policy hop (the S3 bucket policy) as the denying hop, not the service role which is already correct
States Personalize uniquely requires a bucket policy naming personalize.amazonaws.com in addition to the role's S3 policy (both sides required)
Presents this as a specific hop verdict rather than generic 'check your S3 permissions' prose

evals.prompt: Amazon Forecast CreateDatasetImportJob returns InvalidInputException; the RoleArn I passed in S3Config is arn:aws:iam::444455556666:role/forecast-role but my Forecast dataset is in account 111122223333. Walk the chain and classify this.
evals.expected_output: Reports that no authorization hop denied the call and classifies it in the non-denial form ('Not an access denial'): Forecast forbids passing a cross-account role and returns InvalidInputException, not AccessDenied. Fix is using a role in the calling account, not an IAM change.
assertions: Reports that no authorization hop denied and uses the non-denial label ('Not an access denial'), distinguishing InvalidInputException from AccessDenied
Identifies that Forecast forbids passing a role from another account as the cause
Recommends using a role in the calling account rather than an IAM policy change

evals.prompt: Amazon Rekognition StartLabelDetection completes but no SNS notification arrives; the service role uses the AmazonRekognitionServiceRole managed policy and the topic is arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:111122223333:video-done. Walk the chain and classify whether this is a denial.
evals.expected_output: Marks the service-role SNS hop DENIED_BY as an implicit deny: the managed AmazonRekognitionServiceRole policy scopes sns:Publish to AmazonRekognition* topics and video-done does not match. A real IAM denial, not a Rekognition naming rule.
assertions: Classifies it as a real IAM denial (implicit deny / DENIED_BY) from the managed AmazonRekognitionServiceRole policy scoping sns:Publish to AmazonRekognition* topics, not a naming rule
Attributes the deny to the managed policy's resource scope not matching the topic name video-done
Offers both fixes: rename the topic to start with AmazonRekognition, or grant sns:Publish on the exact topic ARN

evals.prompt: My Amazon Transcribe StartTranscriptionJob fails writing output to the bucket I set in OutputBucketName. I gave a Transcribe service role s3:PutObject on that bucket but it still fails. Walk the chain and tell me whose permission is actually missing.
evals.expected_output: Determines the OutputBucketName batch path runs on the CALLER's credentials (no passed service role on this path, so role hops are NOT_APPLICABLE), so the principal that invoked StartTranscriptionJob needs s3:PutObject (and output-KMS permission if set) - the service role is irrelevant here. The DataAccessRoleArn is a different path.
assertions: States the OutputBucketName batch path uses the caller's own credentials, so the service-role hops are NOT_APPLICABLE for this path
Identifies the missing grant as the caller's s3:PutObject on the output bucket (and output-KMS if set), and states the service role is irrelevant on this path
Distinguishes this caller-credentials path from the separate DataAccessRoleArn path
